records.sourceFile: Risk associated with the use of selected ingredients in food supplements.pdf

paper.citation: Jędrejko K, Lazur J, Muszyńska B. Risk Associated with the Use of Selected Ingredients in Food Supplements. Chem Biodivers. 2021;18:e2000686.
paper.abstract: This review covers four newer categories of food supplements sold in Europe, the US, Australia and parts of Asia. It describes contamination, unauthorized and synthetic ingredients, and WADA-prohibited substances, and it links several ingredients to adverse effects and legal issues. The authors conclude that pre-workout, fat burner, brain booster and hormone booster products have the highest risk of harmful content.
paper.tldr: Pre-workout, fat burner, brain booster and hormone booster supplements carry the highest risk of harmful or prohibited ingredients. Athletes should check products carefully before use, especially where doping rules apply.
paper.methods: A narrative review of the chemical, regulatory and doping literature on selected supplement ingredients, with reference to EFSA novel food rules and WADA lists. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: Products in the four categories may contain stimulants, plant ingredients used to disguise stimulants, medicines or synthetic compounds, and substances prohibited by WADA. Some products contain combinations of active ingredients that may cause adverse effects, and some have led to doping sanctions, such as methylsynephrine and higenamine cases traced to supplements.
paper.limitations: No systematic search method is described, and evidence of harm comes from case reports, small volunteer studies and regulatory notifications rather than systematic outcome data. Prevalence figures come from heterogeneous surveys, and product contents vary by brand and batch.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes and staff should check pre-workout, fat burner and hormone-related products against WADA lists and be cautious about unlabelled stimulants. The review supports caution over these categories rather than proof of harm from any single product.
paper.athleteDev: Athletes using pre-workout or fat-burning supplements should check ingredients against WADA lists and be aware that products may contain stimulants or hormone-related compounds not clearly declared on the label.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The review contains no rehabilitation or injury-recovery data.

records.sourceFile: Role of ketogenic diet on body composition, physical health, psychosocial well-being and sports performance in athletes - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Bowler AL, Polman R. Role of a Ketogenic Diet on Body Composition, Physical Health, Psychosocial Well-Being and Sports Performance in Athletes: A Scoping Review. Sports. 2020;8:131.
paper.abstract: This scoping review, conducted under JBI methodology, searched several databases and reference lists for studies of ketogenic diets (under 5% of energy from carbohydrate, at least 21 days) in trained athletes. From 814 articles screened, 12 studies met the criteria and covered body composition, physical health, well-being and performance. The authors report beneficial effects on body weight and fat mass, mixed effects on physical health, conflicting results for performance, and well-being benefits only after week two.
paper.tldr: Across 12 small studies of trained athletes, body weight and fat mass fell and fat oxidation rose on a ketogenic diet, but in the one randomized body-composition study the non-KD group lost similar weight. Performance results were mixed and some physical-health markers moved unfavorably, and the authors say the evidence is too limited for firm recommendations.
paper.methods: Scoping review following JBI methodology, searching PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and the Cochrane database from inception to June 2020, plus citation indexes and reference lists. Included studies used a ketogenic diet (under 5% of energy from carbohydrate) for at least 21 days in trained or well-trained athletes, and each was critically appraised with a JBI or related checklist.
paper.findings: The 12 studies included 101 athletes (84 men, 17 women) from seven sports, and the diets ran from three to twelve weeks. Body weight and fat mass fell within the KD groups of the two body-composition studies, but in the randomized taekwondo study the reductions were similar in the non-KD group, and lean mass was unchanged in gymnasts while fat-free mass fell in the taekwondo athletes. Fat oxidation rose in several studies, dietary iron intake was lower in the KD group, and bone resorption markers rose and formation markers fell after three weeks in one study. Performance results conflicted: VO2 peak rose in one study but exercise economy worsened, a 2000 m time improved within the KD group in one taekwondo study, and time to exhaustion was similar in others. Well-being fell in the first two weeks and then improved in one study of endurance athletes.
paper.limitations: The included studies were small (5 to 37 participants), low quality, and mostly cross-sectional or non-randomized, and several reported on the same elite race-walker cohort, which limits generalizability and may over-weight negative findings. Performance was assessed in laboratory conditions rather than competition, and the review does not pool results quantitatively.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff advising athletes who are considering a ketogenic diet should note that body weight and fat mass fell in small studies, while lean-mass, performance and immune effects are unresolved. The authors suggest the diet may suit athletes who struggle to make weight, but that rests on the small body-composition studies, and they recommend monitoring lean mass and consulting each athlete before starting.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff should not assume a ketogenic diet improves performance, since endurance and exercise-economy results were mixed and the one strength study showed no change. If the diet is used, the authors suggest tracking lean mass and adding protein or supplements to protect it, and this review does not test whether those steps work.
paper.rtp: The review contains no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Safety of beta-alanine supplementation in humans - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: de Oliveira EP, Artioli GG, Burini RC. Safety of beta-alanine supplementation in humans: a narrative review. Sport Sciences for Health. 2023.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of the safety of beta-alanine supplementation, covering paresthesia and the evidence on liver, kidney, taurine and long-term outcomes.
paper.tldr: Beta-alanine appears safe at recommended doses in healthy people for up to about six months. The main side effect is tingling (paresthesia), which can be reduced by smaller or slow-release doses.
paper.methods: Narrative review rather than a systematic search. The authors summarise clinical and safety studies, a systematic review and meta-analysis, a review on military personnel and the International Society of Sports Nutrition and Australian Institute of Sport positions.
paper.findings: No adverse events were linked to beta-alanine in the reviewed literature. Paresthesia is the main side effect, is dose-related, and can be reduced with single doses under 800 mg or sustained-release forms. A meta-analysis found no effect on skeletal muscle taurine and only a small rise in alanine aminotransferase that stayed within clinical reference ranges.
paper.limitations: Most studies were not designed to assess safety, some lacked key safety information, and none ran beyond 6 months; the clinical-marker studies used 3.2 g per day or less for 12 weeks or less. The paresthesia dose threshold is given as under 1.6 g in the abstract but under 800 mg in the body and conclusion. One author declared links to a beta-alanine supplement company (Natural Alternatives International).
paper.practicalImplications: The evidence supports safety at recommended doses for up to 6 months. Splitting doses or using slow-release products reduces tingling, but the safety of chronic high-dose use or use beyond 6 months has not been studied.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Athletes can use beta-alanine within recommended doses, and split or slow-release forms reduce paresthesia. The review notes that the ergogenic effect applies to exercise of about 0.5 to 10 minutes.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Seasonal changes in free 25-(OH)D and vitamin D metabolite ratios and their relationship with psychophysical stress markers in male professional football players.pdf

paper.citation: Książek A, Zagrodna A, Lombardi G, Słowińska-Lisowska M. Seasonal changes in free 25-(OH)D and vitamin D metabolite ratios and their relationship with psychophysical stress markers in male professional football players. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1258678.
paper.abstract: Free 25-(OH)D, bioavailable 25-(OH)D, vitamin D metabolite ratios and stress markers were measured six times in 20 male professional football players over half a year. Total 25-(OH)D, bioavailable 25-(OH)D, vitamin D binding protein and several metabolites showed a seasonal rhythm, while free 25-(OH)D and the stress markers did not. Free and total 25-(OH)D were not correlated with the stress markers, so free measurement showed no advantage in this group.
paper.tldr: In one club of professional footballers, total and bioavailable vitamin D were higher in summer than winter. Free vitamin D and the stress markers did not follow a seasonal pattern and were not linked to each other.
paper.methods: Longitudinal observational study of 20 male professional players from one club, after excluding injured players, those missing more than two draws, and regular calcium or vitamin D supplement users. Blood was drawn in June (V1), July (V2), August (V3), October (V4), December (V5) and January (V6) across pre-season, competitive season and off-season. Total 25-(OH)D metabolites were measured by LC-MS/MS, VDBP by ELISA, and free and bioavailable 25-(OH)D were calculated. Stress markers included ferritin, liver enzymes, CK, testosterone, cortisol and T/C ratio. Mixed models, cosinor rhythm analysis and Pearson correlations were used.
paper.findings: Cosinor analysis showed a seasonal rhythm for VDBP (P=0.003), total 25-(OH)D (P<0.001), bioavailable 25-(OH)D (P<0.001), 24,25-(OH)2D3 (P<0.001), 3-epi-25-(OH)D3 (P<0.001), and the 25-(OH)D3:24,25-(OH)2D3 and 25-(OH)D3:3-epi-25-(OH)D3 ratios. Summer values were higher than winter for VDBP (P=0.013), total 25-(OH)D (P<0.001), bioavailable 25-(OH)D (P=0.006) and 24,25-(OH)2D3 (P<0.001); mean total 25-(OH)D fell from 48.6 ng/mL in August to 33.7 ng/mL in January. Free 25-(OH)D showed no rhythm (P=0.082) and no seasonal difference (P=0.12). No stress marker showed a rhythm, although AST (P=0.027) and ALT (P=0.018) were higher in summer than winter. A strong correlation between 25-(OH)D3 and 24,25-(OH)2D3 was present in each period.
paper.limitations: Twenty of 42 recruited players were analysed, and the data cover only half of a year. Free 25-(OH)D was calculated from total 25-(OH)D and binding constants rather than measured. Training load was described by session type and duration only, so the claim that loads did not affect metabolites is weakly supported. Sporadic vitamin D intake was allowed, and the authors name sunlight exposure as a major driver of vitamin D levels without reporting measuring it. The text and Table 4 also differ on one p-value.
paper.practicalImplications: In this club at 50 to 54 degrees N, total and bioavailable vitamin D fell from summer to winter, although group means stayed above 30 ng/mL. The study did not test monitoring or supplementation, and it does not show that free vitamin D or the stress markers are useful for guiding intake or training.
paper.athleteDev: This study has limited direct performance application. It suggests that total and bioavailable vitamin D in professional footballers tend to be lower in winter, which may matter for planning vitamin D monitoring across the year, and it does not show that stress markers or free vitamin D add to training decisions.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It excluded injured players and did not measure rehabilitation, injury recovery or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Short-Term D-Aspartic Acid Supplementation Does Not Affect Serum Biomarkers Associated With the Hypothalamic– Pituitary–Gonadal Axis in Male Climbers.pdf

paper.citation: Crewther B, Witek K, Zmijewski P, Obmiński Z. Short-Term D-Aspartic Acid Supplementation Does Not Affect Serum Biomarkers Associated With the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis in Male Climbers. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: In a two-period crossover trial, 16 male climbers took 3 g/day of D-aspartic acid or placebo for two weeks. D-aspartic acid did not change serum testosterone, free testosterone or LH, and the only hormonal time effects were a rise in SHBG and a fall in cortisol.
paper.tldr: In 16 male climbers, 3 g/day of D-aspartic acid for two weeks did not change testosterone, free testosterone or LH compared with placebo. Hormone findings in this small group do not support its use to raise testosterone in similar athletes.
paper.methods: Sixteen male climbers (mean age 35.4 years) completed a randomised, single-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial with 3 g/day of D-aspartic acid or placebo for 2 weeks, a 2-week washout, then the reverse order. Serum testosterone, LH, SHBG and cortisol were measured before and after each block, with calculated free testosterone, hand-grip strength, body mass and blood chemistry. Analysis used two-factor repeated-measures ANOVA and Pearson correlations.
paper.findings: D-aspartic acid had no treatment or treatment-by-time effect on testosterone, free testosterone, LH, body mass, grip strength or blood chemistry. Time effects across both conditions were a 6.8% rise in SHBG, a 13.6% fall in cortisol and a 3.1% rise in left-hand grip strength (p=.025). Pre-treatment testosterone was negatively related to its change under placebo but not under DAA, although these correlations did not differ between treatments.
paper.limitations: The study used 16 participants, a two-week dose, a short washout and uncontrolled diet, and the authors note that endogenous DAA was not measured. Performance was assessed only by grip strength and body mass, so the authors' conclusion that DAA gives no ergogenic benefit goes beyond the data.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff advising climbers or similar trained men should know that 3 g/day of D-aspartic acid for two weeks did not change testosterone or LH in this group. The study does not show that the supplement is ineffective for other athletes, doses or durations.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not show a performance benefit or harm, because the only performance-related outcome was hand-grip strength. Its hormone findings suggest no short-term change in testosterone-related markers in trained climbers, which is limited evidence for a training-focused decision.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Participants were healthy and injury-free, and no injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes were studied.

records.sourceFile: Skeletal muscle properties and vascular function do not differ between healthy, young vegan and omnivorous men.pdf

paper.citation: Page J, Erskine RM, Hopkins ND. Skeletal muscle properties and vascular function do not differ between healthy, young vegan and omnivorous men. Eur J Sport Sci. 2021.
paper.abstract: The study compared vascular and skeletal muscle properties between young, healthy, recreationally active habitual vegan (n = 9) and omnivorous (n = 16) men. Vegans consumed less protein, saturated fat and cholesterol. There was anecdotal Bayesian evidence for no differences in FMD, cIMT, vastus lateralis thickness, pennation angle, knee extension MVIC or VO2max, and the authors conclude that a healthy vegan diet is neither beneficial nor detrimental for vascular and muscle health in young untrained men.
paper.tldr: In young untrained men, habitual vegans had similar muscle size, strength, VO2max and vascular function to omnivores despite eating less protein. The sample was small and the evidence for no difference was weak, so it does not settle the question for athletes.
paper.methods: Single-centre cross-sectional study of 25 young men (16 omnivores, 9 vegans of at least six months) with no resistance or endurance training in the prior six months and no more than two hours a week of structured exercise. Measures were brachial FMD and carotid IMT by ultrasound, vastus lateralis thickness and pennation angle, knee extension MVIC on a dynamometer, and VO2max on a cycle ergometer with gas analysis. Diet came from a three-day food diary, and groups were compared with Bayesian independent-groups analysis.
paper.findings: Vegans ate less protein (64 vs 98 g/d; 0.9 vs 1.4 g/kg/d), saturated fat, cholesterol and vitamin B12, and more fibre, iron and vitamin C. Between-group differences in muscle thickness (-1.72 mm, BF01 2.726), pennation angle (BF01 2.844), absolute MVIC (75.93 N, BF01 1.656) and relative VO2max (4.81 mL/kg/min, BF01 1.218) gave only anecdotal evidence for no difference, as did the vascular measures (BF01 1.557 to 2.591). Vegans were older than omnivores (24 vs 21 years, strong evidence).
paper.limitations: The sample was small and limited to young, healthy, untrained men, and diet was recorded over only three days without amino acid analysis. Some abstract values differ from the tables (for example FMD is 3.37% vs 4.58% in the abstract but 6.54% vs 5.32% for vegans vs omnivores in Table 3), and this record uses the table values. The authors note that the lack of age-related decline in this cohort may explain the absence of vascular differences.
paper.practicalImplications: In untrained young men, a habitual vegan diet providing about 0.9 g/kg/d protein was not linked to smaller or weaker thigh muscles or lower VO2max. The study does not test athletes or training adaptation, so it cannot set protein targets for vegan athletes.
paper.athleteDev: This study cannot show how a vegan diet affects training adaptation, because participants were not resistance or endurance trained. The authors themselves suggest protein quality may matter more after resistance exercise in athletes, which this design did not test.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return to sport: the study involved healthy, uninjured, untrained men and measured no injury, rehabilitation or recovery outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Skimmed, lactose-free milk ingestion postexercise - Rehydration effectiveness and gastrointestinal disturbances vs water and a sports drink in physically active people.pdf

paper.citation: Aragón-Vargas LF, Garzón-Mosquera JC, Montoya-Arroyo JA. Skimmed, lactose-free milk ingestion postexercise: rehydration effectiveness and gastrointestinal disturbances versus water and a sports drink in physically active people. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2024.
paper.abstract: This study compared rehydration after moderate-intensity cycling in the heat with water, a sports drink or skimmed lactose-free milk in 16 physically active college students, measuring net fluid balance, diuresis and gastrointestinal symptoms over 3 hours. Milk showed higher fluid retention (about 69%) than water (about 40%), and the sports drink (about 56%) did not differ from either. Gastrointestinal symptoms were mild and did not differ among drinks.
paper.tldr: After a 2% body-mass loss in heat, skimmed lactose-free milk retained more fluid than water over 3 hours, with mild gut symptoms similar to the other drinks. It was not significantly different from a sports drink on fluid retention.
paper.methods: Randomized crossover design in which 16 physically active college students each completed three sessions of cycling in a heat chamber (32 degrees C, 70% relative humidity) to lose about 2% of body mass. They then drank 150% of the loss in three aliquots over 90 minutes, with water, a sports drink or skimmed lactose-free milk, and fluid balance, urine output and gastrointestinal symptoms were measured for 3 hours.
paper.findings: Fluid retention was about 69.8% for milk, 55.6% for the sports drink and 39.6% for water, with only milk versus water significant. Net fluid balance at 3 hours was -0.26 kg for milk, -0.42 kg for the sports drink and -0.67 kg for water; both milk and the sports drink differed from water, while milk and the sports drink did not differ (-0.15 kg, p = .126). Accumulated urine at 3 hours was lower with milk than with the sports drink (313 ml, p < .001) and water (611 ml, p < .001), and gastrointestinal scores were low.
paper.limitations: The sample was small and recreationally active rather than trained athletes, and only one heat exposure with about 2 L of fluid was tested. Milk produced significantly less urine than the sports drink, yet fluid retention and net fluid balance did not differ significantly between them, and the authors report no gastrointestinal differences among drinks although the model's condition main effect was significant (p = .025). The drinks differed in protein, carbohydrate, fat and potassium, so the study cannot say which component drives retention.
paper.practicalImplications: After a moderate sweat loss in heat, skimmed lactose-free milk may be a practical rehydration option if it is tolerated, since it retained more fluid than water and produced less urine than both water and the sports drink. On retention and net fluid balance, milk and the sports drink did not differ significantly, so tolerance and preference remain reasonable deciding factors between them.
paper.athleteDev: In physically active adults rehydrating after exercise in the heat, milk gave better fluid retention than water, so it is a reasonable option for athletes who tolerate it. The study did not test athletes, carbohydrate or electrolyte goals, or later performance, so it does not settle drink choice for performance needs.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return to sport: the participants were physically active students without injury, and the study measured only post-exercise hydration.

records.sourceFile: Skin Tattoos Alter Sweat Rate and        Na+ Concentration.pdf

paper.citation: Luetkemeier MJ, Hanisko JM, Aho KM. Skin tattoos alter sweat rate and Na+ concentration. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2017;49(7):1432-1436.
paper.abstract: The study compared sweat rate and sweat Na+ concentration from tattooed and nontattooed skin in 10 healthy men, using pilocarpine iontophoresis. Tattooed skin produced less sweat (0.18 vs 0.35 mg/cm2/min) and sweat with more sodium (69.1 vs 42.6 mmol/L) than nontattooed skin. The authors conclude that tattooed skin altered sweat function, and the changes did not relate to tattoo age.
paper.tldr: Tattooed skin sweated about half as much as untattooed skin and gave sweat with higher sodium when stimulated at rest. Whether this changes sweat loss or heat tolerance during exercise has not been tested.
paper.methods: Within-person comparison in 10 apparently healthy men with a tattoo of at least 5.2 cm2 on one side of the body and untattooed skin at the contralateral site. Sweat was stimulated by two 5-minute cycles of pilocarpine iontophoresis, collected for 20 minutes on a sweat collection disk, and analyzed for rate (by weight) and sodium (by flame photometry). Tattooed and nontattooed sites were compared with paired t-tests, and tattoo age was correlated with the ratios.
paper.findings: Sweat rate from tattooed skin was 0.18 +/- 0.15 vs 0.35 +/- 0.25 mg/cm2/min for nontattooed skin (p = 0.001), with all 10 men sweating less on the tattooed side (ratio 0.53). Sweat Na+ was 69.1 +/- 28.9 vs 42.6 +/- 15.2 mmol/L (p = 0.02), with nine of ten men higher on the tattooed side. Tattoo age explained less than 1% of the variance in the sweat rate ratio and about 6% of the sodium ratio.
paper.limitations: The sample was 10 men, the stimulus was pilocarpine at rest in a room controlled at 19 to 21 C, and no heat load or exercise was applied. The authors state the mechanism is unclear, that the results are preliminary, and that it is unknown whether similar changes occur with heat stress or internal heat production.
paper.practicalImplications: Under pilocarpine stimulation at rest, tattooed skin produced less sweat with a higher sodium concentration, so heavily tattooed athletes may warrant attention in hot conditions. This has not been tested during exercise or heat stress, so it should not change current hydration plans yet.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not give a performance or training prescription. It suggests tattooed skin may sweat differently, which could matter for heat-training planning, but that needs testing during exercise before it informs practice.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return to sport: participants were healthy non-athletes with no injury, and the study measured sweat function at rest only.

records.sourceFile: Sleep and nutrition interactions -   Implications for athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Doherty R, Madigan S, Warrington G, Ellis J. Sleep and Nutrition Interactions: Implications for Athletes. Nutrients. 2019;11:822.
paper.abstract: This narrative review explores the relationship between sleep and nutrition. Various nutritional interventions have been shown to improve sleep, including high carbohydrate, high glycaemic index evening meals, melatonin, tryptophan-rich protein, tart cherry juice, kiwifruit and micronutrients. The authors state that functional food-based interventions designed to enhance sleep and recovery warrant further investigation.
paper.tldr: Several foods and nutrients have improved sleep in small studies, mostly outside athletic groups. For athletes they are options to test, not proven interventions.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy. It covers sleep physiology, the sleep-nutrition link and specific nutrients: carbohydrate, melatonin, tryptophan-rich protein, antioxidants, tart cherry, kiwifruit, B vitamins and magnesium.
paper.findings: In one study, a high glycaemic index meal eaten four hours before bed cut sleep onset latency to 9.0 min, against 17.5 min after a low glycaemic index meal. In one study of healthy adults, tart cherry juice increased total sleep time by 34 min. In 25 volunteers with sleep disturbance, two kiwifruit an hour before bed for four weeks increased actigraphy sleep duration by 16.9%, with no control group. In six healthy men, melatonin at 0.3 mg or 1 mg shortened sleep onset latency when taken at 6 pm or 8 pm, but 0.3 mg taken at 9 pm lengthened it.
paper.limitations: No systematic search or quality appraisal is described. Several cited trials are small or uncontrolled. The review notes that most antioxidant studies have been done in healthy adults, and that a melatonin, magnesium and zinc supplement will most likely only help where there is a deficiency or insufficiency.
paper.practicalImplications: Evening meal timing and content are low-risk options to test with athletes who struggle to fall asleep. Late caffeine and alcohol are reasonable to limit, given their documented effects on sleep onset, duration and REM sleep. Magnesium and zinc supplements are likely to help only where there is a deficiency, and any supplement should be checked for banned substances.
paper.athleteDev: Use evening food timing and content, plus limits on late caffeine and alcohol, as first sleep steps for athletes. Treat tart cherry, kiwifruit and tryptophan-rich protein as options to trial and track with individual athletes, not as proven interventions.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injured athletes or return to sport, and its sleep findings come mostly from non-athletes. It should not guide return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Specific collagen peptides increase adaptions of patellar tendon morphology following 14-weeks of high-load resistance training  - A randomized-controlled trial.pdf

paper.citation: Jerger S, Centner C, Lauber B, Seynnes O, Friedrich T, Lolli D, et al. Specific collagen peptides increase adaptions of patellar tendon morphology following 14-weeks of high-load resistance training: A randomized-controlled trial. Eur J Sport Sci. 2023;23(12):2329-2339.
paper.abstract: This placebo-controlled study tested 5 g a day of specific collagen peptides (SCP) combined with 14 weeks of resistance training in 50 healthy, moderately active men. The SCP group showed a significantly greater increase in patellar tendon cross-sectional area than placebo at 60% and 70% of tendon length. Both groups increased tendon stiffness, muscle cross-sectional area and strength without significant group differences. Trial registration: DRKS00029244.
paper.tldr: In moderately active men doing 14 weeks of high-load leg training, 5 g a day of collagen peptides enlarged the patellar tendon more than placebo at two sites, but did not change strength or stiffness gains. Treat it as a size effect, not a performance or injury-prevention result.
paper.methods: Monocentric, prospective, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial with block randomisation on baseline tendon area. Participants trained three times a week for 14 weeks at 70% to 85% of 1RM. Patellar tendon cross-sectional area was measured by MRI at 10% intervals along the tendon, and stiffness, knee extension strength and rectus femoris size were also measured before and after training.
paper.findings: Patellar tendon cross-sectional area rose 10.7% with SCP and 6.5% with placebo within groups, and the time by group interaction was significant only at 60% (P = .019) and 70% (P = .010) of tendon length. Tendon stiffness rose about 20% in both groups, and leg press and knee extension 1RM rose 31% to 37% in both groups with no group difference. Rectus femoris cross-sectional area rose about 5% in both groups with no group difference.
paper.limitations: 19 of 50 recruited men dropped out (9 SCP, 10 placebo), so the analysis rests on the 31 completers, although the abstract says 50 participants completed the program. Only two of eleven tendon sites showed a significant group difference, the study covered men aged 18 to 40 only, and results apply only to this collagen product at 5 g a day for 14 weeks. Part of the costs were paid by Gelita AG, the product's maker.
paper.practicalImplications: Adding 5 g a day of collagen peptides to a 14-week high-load leg training block may increase patellar tendon size more than placebo, at 60% and 70% of tendon length. Stiffness and strength gains were similar in both groups, so no extra strength benefit should be expected.
paper.athleteDev: For athletes doing heavy knee-extensor work, the study suggests a possible extra tendon-size benefit from collagen peptides, but no extra strength or stiffness benefit, and it used non-athletes.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy men with no tendon injury, so it does not show whether collagen peptides help tendon healing or rehabilitation. The authors say clinical trials in patients with tendon injury are needed.

records.sourceFile: Sports Dietitians Australia Position Statement- Nutrition for Exercise in Hot Environments.pdf

paper.citation: McCubbin AJ, Allanson BA, Caldwell Odgers JN, Cort MM, Costa RJS, Cox GR, et al. Sports Dietitians Australia Position Statement: Nutrition for Exercise in Hot Environments. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2020 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Position of Sports Dietitians Australia that exertional heat stress challenges athletes' nutritional status, health and performance. Recommended strategies include heat acclimation, starting exercise euhydrated, pre-exercise hyperhydration by sodium or glycerol loading, monitoring fluid balance and gastrointestinal tolerance, cold beverages and menthol, with tailored plans for youth, endurance and para-sport athletes.
paper.tldr: Heat stress makes hydration, fuelling and gut comfort harder, so athletes should start euhydrated, practise their drinking plan in training and acclimatize where possible. Cold drinks, menthol and hyperhydration can help in some situations and should be tested in the athlete's own setting.
paper.methods: Position statement developed by the authors, who review the physiology of heat stress and summarize practical strategies. No systematic search or formal evidence grading is described.
paper.findings: The statement recommends heat acclimation and starting exercise euhydrated, and says pre-exercise hyperhydration may be desirable in some scenarios, achieved by acute sodium or glycerol loading. It recommends assessing fluid balance, gastrointestinal tolerance and thirst responses. Ice-slurry and cold beverages may help in hot, humid, still conditions but may not in warm, dry, windy settings, and menthol can alter thermal sensation. Table 3 gives sport-specific advice: endurance athletes should practise fluid plans in training and keep carbohydrate intake steady, and para-sport athletes should avoid overhydration.
paper.limitations: The statement is a consensus document with no new data and no described grading system. Its recommendations depend on individual sweat rates, gut tolerance and event rules, and the authors note that sweat characteristics explain less than 20% of the variation in sweat sodium losses between athletes, so generic plans may fall short.
paper.practicalImplications: Measure sweat losses and hydration status in training that mimics the hot event, and practise the fluid and carbohydrate plan there. Use cooling strategies such as cold beverages, ice slurry and pre-cooling where practical, and avoid large fluid volumes for para-sport athletes with impaired sweating.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Heat acclimation, starting euhydrated and practised fluid and carbohydrate plans are the main performance steps. Cold beverages and menthol can improve perceived comfort, though the statement says their value depends on conditions.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Not addressed. The statement covers hot-weather nutrition and hydration and gives no guidance on return after illness or injury, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.
